name: Sanggau
confidence_why: No source describes stress in Sanggau itself: Smith (2019, with Smith 2017 and 2021) says only that the Land Dayak languages, Sanggau among them, are stress-final, and Rensch, Rensch, Noeb and Ridu (2012) describe final stress for the Sarawak Bidayuh, so final stress for Sanggau is an inference from its subgroup, not an attested fact.
catalog_citation: Smith, Alexander D. 2019. A second look at Proto-Land Dayak vowels. Oceanic Linguistics 58(1): 110-142. University of Hawai'i Press typeset PDF (33 pp; PDF title ' 110.142'; copyright line on p. 111) from the author's site. Family-level corroboration: Rensch, Rensch, Noeb & Ridu 2012, The Bidayuh Language: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow (SIL e-Book 33), sec. 6.2.4 p. 292 and sec. 4.1.2 p. 47; Smith 2017, The Languages of Borneo (PhD diss., UH Manoa), sec. 2.8.2 p. 185; Smith 2021, The historical phonology of Hliboi, OL 60(1), fn. 2 p. 134 and sec. 5 p. 154. Glottolog sang1339 page (the verification download) lists no descriptive work.
catalog_locator: Smith 2019 p. 111, last paragraph of sec. 1 (after Table 2), running onto p. 112; fn. 2 on p. 112 for Sanggau's membership in Southern Land Dayak (PDF physical pp. 2-3). Corroboration: Rensch et al. 2012 sec. 6.2.4 p. 292 and sec. 4.1.2 p. 47, p. 94 fn. 79; Smith 2017 sec. 2.8.2 p. 185 (after footer 184); Smith 2021 sec. 5 p. 154 and Table 23.
catalog_quote: From a historical point of view, the existence of a full/reduced vowel distinction in the penultimate syllable is unexpected for two reasons: 1) the modern Land Dayak languages are stress-final, a pattern which is likely reconstructable to the proto-language. It is typologically unexpected for unstressed vowels to have a greater number of distinctions than stressed vowels. [fn. 2, p. 112] ... Southern Land Dayak includes Golik, Kembayan, Jangkang, Ribun, and Sanggau, among others. [Smith 2017: 185] Most importantly, stress in many of the languages of West Kalimantan is consistently word-final, a feature of most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area. [Rensch et al. 2012: 292] ... an accentual difference is not evident in the contemporary Land Dayak languages. They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position. [Smith 2021: 154] Although not all LD languages were affected by stress shift in this way, Hliboi demonstrates the potential for typologically uncommon change to arise from this type of stress realignment.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (extracted text run on the PDF itself, pp. 2-3 of the file = printed pp. 111-112): "From a historical point of view, the existence of a full/reduced vowel distinction in the penultimate syllable is unexpected for two reasons: 1) the modern Land Dayak languages are stress-final, a pattern which is likely reconstructable to the proto-language. It is typologically unexpected for unstressed vowels to have a greater number of distinctions than stressed vowels." Verbatim on printed p. 111 (only difference: line-break hyphenation "mod-ern"). Fn. 2 (printed p. 112): "Southern Land Dayak includes Golik, Kembayan, Jangkang, Ribun, and Sanggau, among others." Verbatim.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; asserted for the Land Dayak subgroup as a whole (and for 'most' Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area, where Sanggau lies) by the one linguist who has collected first-hand Sanggau data, not stated for Sanggau individually.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Land Dayak/Sanggau (Smith 2017 raises secondary stress only for Merap, a Kayanic language).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Sanggau; Smith 2017 hedges with 'most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area' and describes Hliboi Bidayuh as 'word-final and strong' with vowel breaking as a correlate.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited wordlist citation forms (Smith 2017 fieldwork, 200-item comparative lists); Sanggau transcriptions in Smith 2017 carry no stress marks. Group-level generalization, not a Sanggau-specific phonological description.
new_statements.identity_note: sang1339 / scg is the Land Dayak (Southern Land Dayak; Glottolog 'South Bidayuh') language of Sanggau regency on the Kapuas, with Ethnologue dialects Dosan, Mayau, Sanggau (very heterogeneous, possibly more than one language). It is NOT Sanggau Malay (Malayic), which the Indonesian Wikipedia article 'Bahasa Sanggau' wrongly files under this code. Smith's Sanggau data (the only first-hand modern data found) come from one consultant 'in and around Sanggau' town. The stress statement is at the Land Dayak subgroup level (Smith 2019) / 'most of the Land Dayak languages of the Kapuas River area' (Smith 2017), not a Sanggau-specific description; sibling Hliboi Bidayuh (hlib1234?) is described individually as word-final.

new_statements.quote: The relative chronology in table 23 begins with PLD, where important changes such as the realignment of stress to the final syllable, the shift of *l to PLD *r, and changes to vowel realization are reconstructed (Smith 2019). All four quoted passages are verbatim: printed p. 154 (pdf 23) sec. 5 'The relative chronology in table 23 begins with PLD, where important changes such as the realignment of stress to the final syllable, the shift of *l' continuing on p. 155 'to PLD *r, and changes to vowel realization are reconstructed (Smith 2019).'; Table 23 p. 154 'Stage 1 PLD Stress realignment'; p. 155 (pdf 24) sec. 6 'In Hliboi, like many other languages in Borneo, these changes occurred after stress realignment from trochaic and p…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Smith 2019 statement (stress-final Land Dayak, reconstructable to PLD) and supplies the explicit PLD-stage chronology; Sanggau is covered only by membership in Southern LD, not by any Sanggau-specific sentence or data. Fills the empty catalog rule field indirectly (group-level inference).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress was realigned from the penult to the final syllable already at the Proto-Land Dayak stage (Table 23, Stage 1), so all Land Dayak daughters including Southern LD (where fn. 2 places Sanggau [scg]) inherit final stress; Hliboi (the paper's subject) is described as iambic/word-final. There is no synchronic stress subsection for Hliboi (sec. 3 covers syllable shape, consonants, vowels, vowel breaking), and no Sanggau data at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. The 'not all LD languages were affected by stress shift in this way' (p. 154) refers to the follow-on penult reduction/deletion, not to stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: Neither work describes the Sanggau variety [scg] (Ethnologue dialects Dosan, Mayau, Sanggau) directly. Smith 2021 is about Hliboi (Bau Bidayuh, Bengkayang regency) and names Sanggau [scg] only in fn. 2 as a Southern Land Dayak member. Rensch et al. 2012 describes Sarawak Bidayuh dialects (Singai, Jagoi, Biatah, Bukar-Sadung etc.) and extends the final-accent statement to 'the contemporary Land Dayak languages' as a group; its appendix inventory lists Sanggau-regency wordlists (Ribun, Kembayan, Galik, Tanap, Jongkang, Mayan, Muduk, Bisomu, Peruan, Tebuas) but no variety labelled Sanggau/Dosan/Mayau, and 'Sanggau-Ledo' (Bryant 1990) is a Bakati' area unrelated to scg. The fixed: final syllable reading for sang1339 therefore rests on group-level statements about Land Dayak / Southern Land Dayak, not on Sanggau-specific data; catalog should mark the placement as inferred from the subgroup.

new_statements.quote: In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). [p. 47] ... In such words initiation of stress (accent) on the ultima vowel is usually perceptible: (C)V1.ˈV1(C). [p. 47] ... Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached. [p. 94 fn. 79] ... an accentual difference is not evident in the contemporary Land Dayak languages. They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position. [p. 292]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (final) as the existing Smith 2019 statement, and Smith 2019 cites this work as a data source. Refines slightly by hedging to citation forms and adding the clitic-stress remark. Describes Sarawak Bidayuh dialects and Land Dayak as a group; no data for the Sanggau variety [scg] itself (Sanggau regency appears only in the Pusat Bahasa wordlist inventory, and 'Sanggau-Ledo' in Bryant 1990 is a different place, Bakati' territory).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the ultima (final syllable) of the stem, at least in citation forms and especially utterance-finally; the authors hedge on connected speech ('perhaps in context'). Enclitics attached to a word take the stress. Stated for Bidayuh (Sarawak) in Part 1 and generalised to all contemporary Land Dayak languages in sec. 6.2.4, where the full/reduced penult-vowel contrast is derived from an earlier (PAN-era) accentual contrast that no longer exists.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress statement is hedged to citation forms/utterance-final position; in (C)V1.V1(C) words of western dialects and Rara the accent onset on the ultima is 'usually perceptible' (p. 47); no exceptions to final stress are listed. The penult full/reduced vowel contrast is explicitly said not to be an accentual difference today (p. 292).
new_statements.identity_note: Neither work describes the Sanggau variety [scg] (Ethnologue dialects Dosan, Mayau, Sanggau) directly. Smith 2021 is about Hliboi (Bau Bidayuh, Bengkayang regency) and names Sanggau [scg] only in fn. 2 as a Southern Land Dayak member.
